# ADR-003: The documentation site is generated by a plain Bun script, not a framework

**Date:** 2026-08-04
**Status:** Accepted

## Status

Accepted

## Context

PRD-005 (FEAT-TOOL-003) makes the protocol legible to outsiders: a public
site whose pages are rendered from the repo at build time, embedding the
existing viewer as a live playground. SP-005 requires that any tooling the
site build needs be justified by a recorded decision rather than added
silently. This is that decision.

Research 11 measured, rather than assumed, what the candidates cost. Every
candidate was installed and built on this machine with the real
`tools/viewer/dist/index.html` placed in its passthrough directory.

Two facts came back that constrain the choice, and one that does not.

**Does not constrain:** the CSP. All seven static-site generators copied the
viewer byte-exact — sha256 identical in every `dist/` — so its self-carried
`<meta http-equiv="Content-Security-Policy">` survives untouched and the
`sha256-…` hashes stay valid. No candidate needs an iframe; each has a
verbatim passthrough directory. Embedding the playground was expected to be
the hard part. It is not.

**Does constrain:** the dependency footprint. Measured transitive package
counts — Eleventy 130, VitePress 127, Astro 202, Starlight 362, Docusaurus
1,275 — against `accept.sh:22` (DEP-FREEZE), which asserts the exact
two-entry dependency dict and exactly two `go.mod` requires. Every
JavaScript framework fails that gate; none of them fails any other
constraint.

**Also constrains, separately:** no off-the-shelf JSON Schema renderer
survives contact with our schema. Run against the real 58 KB core schema —
2020-12, root is `$ref: "#/$defs/recipe"`, 30 `$defs`, recursive via
components, 93 `description` strings totalling 17,519 characters — the best
result (json-schema-for-humans) renders 89 of 93 descriptions, silently
dropping the `$defs` description whenever the referencing property has its
own. That is precisely the prose defining what a `variantDiscriminator`
*is*. Two other tools mangle it further; `json-schema-static-docs`
stack-overflows because it fully dereferences and we are recursive.

Daniel's direction (2026-08-04), when shown the tooling options, moved the
criterion: *"I don't care much which tool or tools we use. My MUST have is
the best to act as a manual of the protocol and easy to understand and
navigate, a good looking and easy to understand documentation overall and a
good validator and viewer."* On packages: *"just make sure they are stable,
safe, small as possible and maintained."*

So the deciding question is not "which framework is lightest" but "which
path produces the best manual." That reframing matters, because the features
a framework actually buys — sidebar navigation, search, a responsive theme,
typographic defaults — are exactly the MUST-haves.

## Decision

**The site is generated by a plain Bun script in `tools/docsite/`, with
`marked` as its single dependency. No documentation framework.**

Rationale, in the order that decided it:

1. **The framework's headline value does not apply to us.** A docs framework
   earns its footprint by turning hand-written Markdown into a navigable
   site. Our content is *generated* and *highly structured* — the navigation
   is derivable from the normative-surface inventory itself, not authored.
   We would be paying 200–1,275 packages for a nav we can compute.

2. **We must hand-roll the schema renderer regardless.** Since no tool
   renders our schema faithfully, the largest single piece of work is ours
   either way. A framework would wrap ~200 lines of custom rendering in 200
   MB of scaffolding.

3. **Zero-dependency data loading is real, not aspirational.** Verified on
   the pinned Bun: `Bun.YAML.parse()` is built in, and `import x from
   './f.yaml'` resolves directly. Every registry entry, example, manifest and
   schema is readable with no dependency at all.

4. **Only the no-framework path can enforce documentation policy.** The build
   can fail on "a `$def` has no description" or "an enum member is
   undocumented" — turning the site build into a protocol-quality gate. No
   framework offers this, and for a protocol repo it is the point.

5. **`marked` fits the stated package bar.** Measured at exactly 1 package
   with no transitive dependencies (markdown-it is 7); actively maintained;
   the reference CommonMark implementation in JS. It is the smallest possible
   widening of the frozen surface, and it buys correct rendering for 427
   lines of normative prose we must not render wrong. A hand-rolled Markdown
   subset was rejected: a spec document is exactly where a subtly wrong
   renderer does damage, and a mangled table in `VERSIONING.md` is a lying
   page — the failure this whole cut exists to prevent.

6. **Relative-path output keeps `file://` working**, matching the viewer's
   existing posture. Astro, Starlight, VitePress and Docusaurus all emit
   root-absolute paths and require a served root; the last three also ship
   client routers that prefetch chunks.

**The dependency freeze widens by exactly one entry**, from two to three, and
DEP-FREEZE is updated to assert the new exact set. The gate stays exact — it
is not relaxed to a maximum.

**Because the framework is not providing navigation, typography or layout,
those become explicit engineering work with their own requirement** — see
FR-DOC-006 in PRD-005. This ADR does not get to claim the no-framework path
is free; it moves that cost from dependencies to design, deliberately.

## Consequences

**Good.** DEP-FREEZE stays meaningful (exact, three entries). No egress by
construction — nothing to strip, nothing to assert away, unlike VitePress
which ships `api.iconify.design` and `docsearch.algolia.com` in its bundle.
The build can enforce protocol documentation quality. Output works from
`file://` and from any dumb bucket. The DIST-FRESH drift pattern already in
`accept.sh` applies unchanged, pointed at the site directory.

**Bad.** Navigation, search, responsive layout and typography are ours to
build and maintain. If the site later needs genuine full-text search across
109 registry entries plus the spec, a generated client-side index is more
work than `pagefind` would have been. We accept this; it is the cost of item
6 above and it is bounded by our page count.

**Risk we are taking on.** The site's quality now depends on design work, not
on a theme's defaults. Daniel's MUST-have is a *manual* — if the hand-rolled
navigation is worse than Starlight's, that is a real regression against the
goal, and no dependency count compensates for it. FR-DOC-006 exists so this
is checked rather than assumed.

**Prerequisite this surfaces.** CI installs Go only
(`.github/workflows/validate.yml`), so it cannot run Bun today. A mise/Bun
setup step is a hard prerequisite for the drift gate running in CI at all.

## Alternatives Considered

### Hugo (single binary, Go — already pinned)
- **Pros:** no npm packages at all; verified reading the real core schema and
  a YAML file at build time; no default theme, so egress is zero by
  construction; could be a `go.mod` tool dependency.
- **Cons:** a second templating language to learn and maintain; adds a
  toolchain to CI; any third-party theme reintroduces egress risk (Docsy
  pulls Google Fonts); still leaves the schema renderer to us.
- **Rejected because:** it solves the dependency problem we can already solve
  with zero, while adding a templating layer between us and output we need
  fine control over — and the schema renderer, the actual work, is unaffected.

### Astro or Starlight, with a recorded DEP-FREEZE exception
- **Pros:** the best data story of the JS candidates — `glob()`/`file()`
  loaders natively parse `.json`, `.yaml`, `.toml`; a plain Astro page builds
  to zero JS and zero external references (verified); Starlight's theme is
  genuinely egress-clean (0 woff2, Pagefind index is local) and would deliver
  Daniel's navigation MUST-have out of the box.
- **Cons:** 202 / 362 packages; requires explicitly widening the gate SP-005
  was written to protect; root-absolute paths break `file://`.
- **Rejected because:** the one thing it genuinely buys — navigation and
  theme — is computable from our own structured inventory, and buying it
  costs 200× the dependency surface. This is the closest call in the set, and
  FR-DOC-006 is what makes rejecting it honest: if we cannot deliver a
  navigable manual by hand, this decision was wrong and should be revisited.

### mdBook
- **Pros:** cleanest egress of all candidates; the only output that works
  from `file://` unmodified; self-hosted fonts, local search index.
- **Rejected because:** it has no build-time data mechanism at all — no way
  to read a JSON Schema and emit pages. We would pre-generate every page with
  a separate script, leaving mdBook doing only chrome. Its `{{#include}}`
  anchors also fail *open*: a missing anchor returns an empty string silently
  (asserted by its own unit test). Silent content loss in a spec is
  unacceptable.
